strengths: Provides a unified theoretical framework covering a wide range of practical stochastic optimizers (SignSGD, Signum, Normalized-SGD, Spectral-SGD, Muon, and their variance-reduced variants) as instances of mini-batch steepest descent under different norms, extending prior full-batch-only implicit bias analyses (e.g., Fan et al. 2025) to the more practically relevant stochastic setting.

Delivers a coherent set of results characterizing how batch size and momentum trade off to determine whether the stochastic algorithm recovers the full-batch max-margin implicit bias, including explicit convergence rates for various learning-rate decay schedules.

The variance-reduction result (recovering the exact full-batch margin for any batch size, at the cost of slower rates) is a clean and intuitive theoretical contribution that ties together the batch-size and momentum findings.

Removes the polynomial dimension dependence present in the closest prior work (Fan et al. 2025) via a sharper entrywise-norm gradient-difference bound, which is a genuine, clearly explained technical improvement.

The batch-size-one analysis on a specially constructed orthogonal dataset is a nice counterexample showing per-sample steepest descent can converge to a qualitatively different (frequency-averaged, not margin-based) solution, which is a conceptually interesting and somewhat surprising finding that tempers the main narrative.
Extension to exponential loss and detailed, largely self-contained proofs in the appendix suggest technical thoroughness and reasonable reproducibility of the theoretical claims.

Synthetic experiments span all algorithm variants (with/without momentum, with/without VR) and three norm geometries (ℓ2, ℓ∞, spectral), and qualitatively corroborate the theoretical predictions (breakdown under small batch without momentum, restoration with large momentum or VR).
weaknesses: All theoretical results are restricted to linear multi-class classifiers on linearly separable data; despite motivating the work through LLM pretraining and Muon/Adam, there is no theoretical or empirical treatment of nonlinear/neural architectures, which substantially limits the practical significance of the claims.

Experiments are entirely synthetic and very small scale (n=200, d=5, 10 classes), with no validation on real datasets or realistic neural network training despite the paper's motivation being large-scale LLM optimization; this leaves a large gap between the paper's stated motivation and its empirical support.

The convergence bounds involve many compounding constants (R, n, m, batch-dependent exponents like m^{2+a}) and rely on reaching a possibly very large threshold time t2 before the stated rates apply; there is little discussion of how large these thresholds/constants are in practice or whether the bounds are informative at realistic scales.

The batch-size-one result, while conceptually interesting, is established only for a specially constructed orthogonal, scale-skewed dataset; it is unclear how much this generalizes to realistic data distributions, and the paper acknowledges this limits any unified theory for the small-batch regime.

The random-reshuffling assumption and momentum drift analysis rely on several technical assumptions (3.3, 3.4) whose practical scope (beyond polynomial learning-rate schedules) is not extensively discussed or justified beyond citing that they are 'commonly used.'

Given the substantial overlap in spirit with concurrent work (Baek et al. 2025 on per-sample Adam), the paper's novelty is somewhat incremental in framing, even though the technical execution (dimension-free rates, general norms, VR analysis) differs and improves upon it.

The paper's presentation is very dense, with the main text mostly summarizing results whose substance and nuance are deferred to a ~50-page appendix; some threshold-time and constant definitions (e.g., t0, t1, t2) are introduced somewhat implicitly and could be clarified for readability.

strengths: Addresses a novel and timely gap: extending implicit bias theory of norm-induced steepest descent (SignSGD, Muon, Normalized-SGD) from full-batch to the mini-batch stochastic setting, relevant to modern LLM optimizers.
Unified framework covering a wide range of algorithms and stabilization mechanisms (momentum, SVRG-style variance reduction) under general entry-wise/Schatten-p norm geometries.
The negative result on lack of momentum (full-batch necessity) is substantiated by a concrete, rigorous counterexample at m=2 (Proposition 4.2), not just a loose sufficient condition.
Technical improvement of independent interest: removes dimension dependence present in prior work (Fan et al. 2025) via tighter global norm bounds on gradient differences.
Extensive theoretical apparatus with detailed, careful appendix proofs, including explicit non-asymptotic constants (e.g., Lemma C.15) supporting reproducibility of theoretical claims.
Reasonably thorough empirical validation across three norms and multiple batch/momentum settings on synthetic data, plus a supporting MNIST experiment with a two-layer nonlinear network.
weaknesses: Entire analysis restricted to linear classifiers on linearly separable data; the practical motivation (deep network training with Muon/SignSGD) is not theoretically covered, and the MNIST experiment (two-layer nonlinear network) is only an empirical, unsupported extension.

The batch-size-1 implicit bias result (Theorem 4.10) relies on a specially engineered orthogonal scale-skewed dataset, limiting generality; the broader claim that no unified small-batch implicit bias theory exists is only suggestively, not rigorously, supported.

Derived convergence rates are complex and involve conservative multiplicative factors (e.g., m/(1-β1), m^{2+a}/(1-β1)) without matching lower bounds, making it hard to assess tightness or practical relevance.

Significant technical machinery (proxy function G(W), core geometric lemmas) is directly inherited from Fan et al. 2025's full-batch framework, making the overall proof architecture incremental; novelty is concentrated in the stochastic noise/momentum/SVR bias bounding lemmas.

Some derived conditions for momentum to help are impractically restrictive (e.g., 1-β1 = O(n^{-3}) needed for b=Ω(1)), and the paper does not discuss whether commonly used momentum values would satisfy the theoretical guarantees for realistic dataset sizes.
Experiments confirm qualitative trends but do not quantitatively verify the tightness or specific scaling (in n, m, β1) of the derived theoretical rates.
Dense notation and heavy reliance on forward references to appendix-defined constants reduce readability of the main text.
